666.title: The unseen
666.hook: believing in what isn't seen is where faith starts (2:3)
666.howItsDone: Muslims describe faith (iman) as belief in Allah, the angels, the revealed books, the messengers, the Last Day and divine decree, much of it in the unseen; classical scholars warned against fortune-telling as a claim on what only Allah knows.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mala'ikah, the angels, and your line, the ones who write. Angels are part of something larger the Qur'an names right at its start.

A short list of things you trusted today without seeing them. The signal that carried your messages. The pilot of a plane you heard overhead. The person who cooked food you bought. The air in the room, which you breathed several hundred times and never once looked at. Trust in what you can't see isn't strange. Nobody gets through a Tuesday without it. And when the Qur'an describes the people it's meant for, on its second page, the very first quality it names is exactly that.

Al-Baqarah begins by calling the book a guidance for those who keep their duty, and then describes them. Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, starts: "Who believe in the Unseen." Before prayer, before giving, the first thing named is what they trust. The Arabic is al-ghayb. The root gh-y-b means to be absent, hidden from view; a student who misses class is gha'ib, absent. So the unseen isn't the imaginary. It's what is real but not in front of you. What's in it? A well-known hadith in Sahih Muslim, where Jibril comes as a stranger and questions the Prophet, lists the heart of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the measuring out of good and bad. Almost all of it sits in the unseen. And the Qur'an is honest about who holds it. Surah six says that with Allah are the keys of the unseen, and no one knows them but Him. It adds a small, startling picture: not a leaf falls but He knows it. Surah twenty-seven says no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah. That's why classical scholars were firm about fortune-tellers: a hadith in Sahih Muslim warns that whoever consults one to ask about hidden things has their prayer unaccepted for forty nights. So faith in the unseen has two sides. It trusts what can't be seen. And it doesn't pretend to see it. The future, the hidden, the leaf before it falls: those stay with Allah.
screen: `TRUST IT, DON'T CLAIM TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes so the seen goes quiet, and feel your breath coming in: you can't see the air, but you're living on it. Pick one unseen thing to rest your weight on for the rest of this sit: your breath, someone's love for you, or, if you believe, Allah's care. Don't try to picture it; just lean on it.
The unseen. Al-ghayb, from gh-y-b, absent: what is real but out of view, the first thing named in al-Baqarah's picture of faith. Today's word.
Your line: faith in the unseen. The keys stay with the One who holds them. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: A healing and a mercy
667.hook: We send down in the Qur'an what is a healing and a mercy (17:82)
667.howItsDone: In ruqyah, Muslims recite the Fatiha, the last two surahs and other verses over someone who is ill, alongside medical treatment; a hadith in al-Bukhari says Allah sent down no disease without its cure.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the unseen, and your line, faith in the unseen. Today, what the book says it does for the one who hears it.

A desert camp, somewhere in Arabia. A small band of the Prophet's companions has stopped near a tribe that won't host them. That night the tribe's chief is stung by a scorpion, and nothing they try helps. Someone comes over: does any of you know a cure? One companion says he does. He sits by the chief and recites the Fatiha over him, again and again, blowing lightly as he goes. The hadith, in al-Bukhari, says the chief got up as if he'd been freed from a rope.

Back in Medina, they told the Prophet ﷺ, and he asked the reciter: how did you know it was a ruqyah, a recitation for healing? He approved what they'd done. That story sits behind a word the Qur'an uses about itself. Surah seventeen, verse eighty-two, in Pickthall's translation: "And We reveal of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for believers." The word for healing is shifa'. Elsewhere the Qur'an calls itself a healing for what is in the breasts, the hearts, in surah ten, and a guidance and a healing in surah forty-one. Notice which sickness these verses point to first. Commentators say it's in the heart: doubt, fear, grief, a restless mind. The book is a mercy for that. Scholars also cite hadith like the scorpion story to hold that its recitation can be a means of healing for the body. And Islamic teaching doesn't set this against medicine. A hadith in al-Bukhari says Allah has not sent down a disease without sending down a cure for it. So shifa' comes in two hands at once: a doctor's prescription in one, a verse in the other. Neither has to cancel the other out. On a low day, the second hand is the one people sometimes forget they have.
screen: `MEDICINE IN ONE HAND, A VERSE IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: You don't have to be low right now; this is practice for the day you are. Bring to mind a short verse or line you know, the Fatiha or anything from this year that stayed with you, or simply the words a healing and a mercy. Say it slowly three times, letting each word take a full breath, and notice whether anything in your chest loosens, even a little.
Shifa'. Healing. The Qur'an calls itself a healing and a mercy for believers, first for the heart, and recited, by the hadith, for the body too. Today's word.
Your line: a healing. One line, held close, for the low days ahead. Until tomorrow.

668.title: Knowledge in the book
668.hook: the first word is read, and knowledge is praised throughout
668.howItsDone: Muslims treat seeking knowledge as a religious duty; some recite "my Lord, increase me in knowledge" (20:114) before study, and hadith scholarship developed careful methods for checking who transmitted a report.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shifa', and your line, a healing. Today, a theme that starts with the very first word revealed.

If you had to guess the first word of a holy book's revelation, you might guess pray, or believe, or obey. In the Islamic account, the angel Jibril comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in a cave on Mount Hira, and the first word is none of those. It's iqra'. Read. Or recite. Surah ninety-six, in Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." A revelation whose first word is read. From there, knowledge runs through the whole of it.

The word is 'ilm, knowledge. Its root, '-l-m, gives a whole family: 'alim, one who knows; its plural, 'ulama', the scholars; mu'allim, a teacher; and al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, one of the names of Allah. In al-Baqarah, the first human, Adam, is honored by being taught: Allah taught him the names of all things, and the angels admit they know only what they've been taught. Surah thirty-nine asks a question that doesn't need answering: "Are those who know equal with those who know not?" In surah fifty-eight, Allah raises in degrees those who believe and those given knowledge. And in surah twenty, the Prophet himself is told to ask for more of it: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Some commentators note it's the only thing he is told to ask more of. The hadith carry it on. One, in Ibn Majah, says seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim. Another, in Sahih Muslim, says whoever walks a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for them a path to the Garden. And here's a line people repeat that isn't in the sources: seek knowledge even as far as China. It's often quoted, and hadith scholars judged it weak or invented. Which is itself a lesson in 'ilm: knowing includes checking. Muslim scholars built a whole science around asking who said a thing, and whether it was really said.

Ask yourself: what's one thing I'd like to understand better? A word from this year's lessons, a skill, a question about someone you love. Pick it and hold it, and if you pray, say the Prophet's line from surah twenty: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
'Ilm. Knowledge, from '-l-m, the root of scholar, teacher and the All-Knowing: what the Prophet is told to ask more of. Today's word.
Your line: seek knowledge. Read first, and check what you read. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: Signs in nature
669.hook: the camel, the bee, the ant, the spider, rain, stars: nature as a book of signs
669.howItsDone: Muslims call each verse of the Qur'an an ayah, a sign, and the same word is used for the signs in creation; reflection on nature (tafakkur) is a long-standing devotional practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ilm, and your line, seek knowledge. Today, the book points away from its own pages.

"Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" That's surah eighty-eight, in Pickthall's translation. Its first hearers rode camels, traded with them, drank their milk, and knew every habit and every sound they made. The question doesn't point them to a vision, or a miracle, or a far-off sky. It points to the animal kneeling at the edge of the tent. Look at that, it says. Look at the thing you see every day.

The word the Qur'an keeps using for this is ayah. It's the word for a verse of the Qur'an. But it also means a sign, a mark that points beyond itself. The same word names a line of scripture and a sunset. Then the book fills a whole zoo with it. Several surahs carry animal names: the Cow, the Bee, the Ant, the Spider, the Elephant. The bee is inspired by its Lord to build homes in hills and trees and bring out a drink of many colors. An ant calls out a warning to its colony so they won't be crushed, and a prophet smiles at it. The spider's house is called the frailest of houses. Rain comes down on dead ground and brings it back. Stars are set for travelers to find their way by in the dark. And again and again, a passage like these ends with a phrase like: in this are signs for people who reflect, or who use their reason, or who listen. In surah three, the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the night and day taking turns, are signs for people of understanding. Some Muslim thinkers put it this way: there are two books open at once, the written one and the created one, and each helps you read the other. In these passages, noticing the world isn't a distraction from faith. The book keeps sending its listeners back outside.
screen: `THE BEE, THE ANT, THE SPIDER, THE RAIN.`

segments.voice: Take a slow walk outside, or sit by a window, and let your eyes stop on one living thing: an ant on the pavement, a bird, a tree, a cloud, a weed in a crack. How is it made, what does it need, what is it doing right now without any help from you? Read it the way you'd read a line of a verse.
Ayah. The Qur'an's word for both a verse and a sign: camels, bees, ants, spiders, rain and stars, all pointing beyond themselves. Today's word.
Your line: the world is signs. Two books open at once, as some Muslim thinkers put it. See you tomorrow.

670.title: Water all through it
670.hook: rain, springs, rivers of the garden: water as mercy all through the book
670.howItsDone: Muslims wash with water (wudu) before prayer and are taught to use little of it, following hadith about the Prophet's small measure; saying bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after is a common practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ayah, and your line, the world is signs. Today, one sign that runs through the whole book like a river.

Turn on a tap. It's the most forgettable act of the day: brushing teeth, filling a kettle, rinsing a cup. The Qur'an was first heard in the Hijaz, where a well could decide whether a town existed, and a caravan's route ran from one water source to the next. There, water isn't background. It's life and death. And it flows through the book, from the making of living things to its pictures of the Garden.
screen: `A LAND WHERE A WELL MAKES A TOWN.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning of things. Surah twenty-one says Allah made every living thing from water. Surah eleven pictures His throne upon the water before the heavens and earth were made. Then the rain. Surah seven describes the winds sent ahead as good news, going before His mercy, and that mercy is the rain: clouds driven to a dead land, and out of it every kind of fruit. Rain and mercy share a sentence. Springs burst from rock when Musa strikes it with his staff, twelve of them, one for each tribe. And at the far end of the book, the Garden is again and again called gardens beneath which rivers flow; surah forty-seven names rivers of water that never goes stale. Water is in the daily life of the faith too. No prayer without washing first, the wudu: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. And a detail that surprises people: a hadith in al-Bukhari says the Prophet ﷺ would do his whole wudu with about one mudd of water, roughly two cupped handfuls, and bathe with a few times that. Another hadith, in Abu Dawud, says Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. So water in Islamic teaching is a mercy from above, a trust held in common, and something not to be poured away. The same tradition that promises rivers remembers a Prophet who used a handful well.

Hold a glass of water, or picture one, and look at it before you drink: a cloud, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Then drink slowly, in small sips, with a breath between each. If you'd like, begin as Muslims are taught to, with bismillah, and finish with alhamdulillah.
Wudu. The washing before prayer, hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet, done by the Prophet with about two cupped handfuls of water. Today's word.
Your line: water is mercy. About two handfuls, used well, were enough for him. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Maryam, the only woman named
671.hook: Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an, and a surah bears her name
671.howItsDone: Muslims honor Maryam as one of the greatest women; Maryam is a common name for Muslim girls, and surah Maryam is widely recited and memorized.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wudu, and your line, water is mercy. Today a new thread through the book: its women.

Read the Qur'an looking only for women, and you'll find a lot of them. A queen who rules a kingdom. A mother who sets her baby on a river. A wife who argues her case and is heard. A wife who laughs at the news that she'll have a son. They speak, they choose, they pray. But almost none of them is named. They're the wife of, the mother of, the sister of, a woman. Except one. Her name appears more often in the Qur'an than in the whole New Testament, and a surah is called by it.

Maryam. Mary, the mother of 'Isa, Jesus. By the usual count her name appears thirty-four times, and surah nineteen bears it. Why her? The Qur'an doesn't explain its choice, and scholars have offered reasons rather than one answer. But look at how it speaks of her. In Al 'Imran the angels say: Allah has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of all the worlds. As a girl in the temple's prayer niche, she's found with provision no one brought her, and when Zakariyya asks where it came from, she answers simply: from Allah. Then the hardest scene. Surah nineteen says the pains of labor drove her, alone, to the trunk of a palm tree, and she cried that she wished she'd died before this and been forgotten. Forgotten, of all words. And she's answered: a stream is set beneath her, the palm will drop fresh dates if she shakes it, so eat, drink and be comforted. When she brings the child home and her people accuse her, she doesn't argue. She points to the baby, and the baby speaks. One more detail. Her son is called, again and again, 'Isa ibn Maryam, Jesus son of Mary. In a culture that named people by their fathers, he is named by his mother. Christians honor her too, with their own ways of speaking about her. In the Qur'an, the woman who feared being forgotten is the one whose name it keeps.
screen: `CHOSEN ABOVE THE WOMEN OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Let one woman come to mind whose care made you who you are, a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, a neighbor, even if few people know it. Say her name slowly, and recall one specific thing she did: a meal, a word, a night she sat up with you. If she has died and you pray, you can ask mercy for her; if she's alive, just hold her in mind with thanks.
Maryam. The only woman named in the Qur'an, chosen above the women of the worlds, and the mother whose name her son carries. Today's word.
Your line: named. Named about thirty-four times, and a surah of her own. Day six hundred seventy-one, done.

672.title: Asiya in Pharaoh's house
672.hook: Pharaoh's wife, who kept faith in the harshest house (66:11)
672.howItsDone: Muslims honor Asiya, with Maryam, as a woman the hadith says reached perfection; her prayer in 66:11 is learned and recited as a du'a, including in hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maryam, and your line, named. Today, a woman the Qur'an never names, and sets beside Maryam anyway.

A hard address for a person of faith: not a desert, not a prison, but a palace. The palace of the man who declared himself lord most high, who had the baby boys of a whole people killed. And inside it, married to him, a woman who believed. The Qur'an calls her only the wife of Pharaoh. Tradition gives her the name Asiya. She first appears when a chest is pulled out of the river.

Surah al-Qasas tells it. Pharaoh's household pulls a baby out of the river, the baby Musa. In a house that kills boys, his wife speaks first: he'll be a comfort of the eye for me and for you, don't kill him; maybe he'll be useful to us, or we'll take him as a son. Her first recorded words save a prophet's life. In surah sixty-six she speaks again, and this time it's a prayer. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Build for me a home with Thee in the Garden." She goes on to ask to be saved from Pharaoh and his deeds, and from a wrongdoing people. The Qur'an sets her up as an example for all believers, and in the next verse sets Maryam beside her: one in a palace, one under a palm. Notice the order of her words in Arabic: rabbi-bni li 'indaka baytan fil-jannah. 'Indaka, with You, comes before baytan, a house. Some scholars sum that detail up with an old saying: the neighbor before the house. What happened to her, the Qur'an doesn't say. Commentators tell stories of her suffering for her faith; those come from later reports, not from the verse. What the hadith does say, in al-Bukhari, is that many men reached perfection, but among women only Maryam and Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh. The Qur'an never shows her leaving that house. It shows her keeping her faith inside it, and saving a child while she was there.

Think of the place in your life that's hardest to be good in, a job, a family table, a group chat, somewhere you can't simply walk out of. Ask what one small thing you could protect there, the way Asiya protected a baby: a kind word, a boundary, a quiet prayer, someone weaker than you. If you pray, you can say her line: my Lord, build for me a home with You.
Asiya. Pharaoh's believing wife, who saved the baby Musa and prayed for a home with Allah, with You before the house. Today's word.
Your line: faith in pharaoh's house. With You first, then the house. See you tomorrow.

recall: for love of Him, or despite loving it

chat.says: Who was Pharaoh's wife in the Qur'an? Was she on his side?
options: No: she believed, saved baby Musa, and prayed for a home with Allah.
Yes: she urged him on, and shared his fate at the very end.
She's never mentioned; the Qur'an tells only of Pharaoh himself.
chat.meaning: Inside Pharaoh's palace she saved Musa and prayed, my Lord, build for me a home with You; the Qur'an makes her an example for believers.

Asiya.meaning: tradition's name for Pharaoh's believing wife
